title: Digitalisation and Digital Transformation in Tax Administrations
text:
Digitalisation and Digital Transformation in Tax Administrations
12 November 2026

Abstract
This report provides an overview of the extent of the use of technology by tax administrations. It brings together the data from 108 economies included in the Inventory of Tax Technology Initiatives and groups them by geographical regions to facilitate the comparison of progress, the understanding of current developments, and the identification of emerging practices. Its primary purpose is to assist tax administrations when considering possible domestic reforms as well as to help identify where future collaboration between tax administrations might be of most value.

Executive summary
Since the OECD’s Forum on Tax Administration (FTA) set out the Tax Administration 3.0 vision in 2020 (OECD, 2020), many tax administrations have accelerated their digital transformation, expanding the use of technology to improve efficiency, enhance compliance, and reduce taxpayer burden. Increasingly, administrations are working towards more seamless, integrated, and user-centric tax systems.
Drawing on data from the Inventory of Tax Technology Initiatives (ITTI) covering 108 tax administrations, this report examines progress in digitalisation and transformation both globally and across regions.

Key findings include:
Digital identity as a foundation: Most taxpayers, particularly in Asia and Europe, now access tax administration services through digital identities.
Integration and user-centric services: More than 80% of administrations covered by the inventory are developing application programming interfaces (APIs). Automation of processes and interactions continues to expand, including through the early adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). Uptake is highest in North, South and West Europe and East and South Asia.
Data-driven administration: Around 60% of administrations receive data directly from taxpayer’s business systems.
Pre-filled tax returns: Many administrations now offer fully pre-filled personal income tax returns for parts of the taxpayer population.
Collect once, use many times: More than 80% of administrations exchange bulk information with other government agencies.
The growing importance of artificial intelligence: Nearly half of administrations, particularly in Central and West Asia and Europe, use AI to strengthen compliance and improve taxpayer services. The most common applications include fraud detecting and risk assessment. Most administrations report having implemented limitations, governance arrangements, and ethical safeguards to support the responsible use of AI.
Skills and organisational change: While many administrations are beginning to identify the skills needed to support digital transformation, comprehensive workforce planning remains limited.
Strategic governance and delivery: Approximately three-quarters of administrations have a digital transformation strategy.

Overall, the data suggests that tax administrations are making significant progress in their digital transformation journeys. As the digital transformation continues to reshape economies and public services, future updates to the ITTI database will provide valuable insights into the pace, direction, and consistency of transformation across tax administrations worldwide.
